Ultimately of uncertain origin.
Compare Old Danish drup (“cud”) (also recorded as drub), older Danish drøff and dreff, and dialectal Swedish dröp (“cud”). These forms are associated with a verb meaning “to chew again, ruminate”; compare Old Swedish drypja and dialectal Swedish drypja, dröpja and drövja. The deeper origin is uncertain. Den Danske Ordbog (“The Danish Dictionary”) tentatively considers Old Danish drup most likely related to dryppe (“to drip”), while the older Ordbog over det danske Sprog (“Dictionary of the Danish Language”) instead proposes a formation containing an element mean

25388.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse há (“aftergrass”), from Proto-Norse ᚺᚨᚺᚨ (haha, “aftergrass”), from Proto-Germanic *hah(w)ō (“aftergrass”).
Compare Icelandic há (“aftergrass”), Norwegian Nynorsk hå (“aftergrass”) and Faroese hógvur (“remaining stubble of cut grass”). / Inherited from Old Norse hár (“spiny dogfish”). The further origin is uncertain. De Vries connects the Old Norse word with an earlier form related to *hōhô (“plow”), perhaps with reference to the jagged form of a shark; another proposal compares *hawwaną (“to hew, cut”).
The same Old Norse word was borrowed as Middle Dutch haeye (“shark”), whence Dutch haai (“shark”); Bokmål later borrowed the Dutch word as hai (“shark”). Doublet of hai (“shark”).
Compare Icelandic hár (“dogfish”), Faroese Faroese háur and hávur (“shark”), and Norwegian Nynorsk hå (“spiny dogfish”).

1005100.etyen:
PIE word
 *tréyes
Compound of tre (“three”) + fork (“fork, forked pole”), literally “three-fork”.
The first component tre (“three”) is from Old Norse þrír (“three”), from Proto-Germanic *þrīz (“three”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes (“three”).
The second component fork (“fork, forked pole”) is from Old Norse forkr (“boathook; stake, pole”), itself borrowed from Latin furca (“fork, pitchfork; fork-shaped support or pole”). The further origin of the Latin word is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk trefork and Danish trefork (“trident”).
